Cells must divide twice during meiosis to achieve two critical goals: reducing the chromosome number by half and creating genetic diversity. Here's why both divisions are essential:

## The Problem Meiosis Solves

Sexual reproduction requires that two parent cells (gametes) fuse together. If these cells had the same number of chromosomes as body cells, the offspring would have twice as many chromosomes as their parents. This doubling would continue with each generation, which isn't sustainable.

## Why Two Divisions Are Necessary

### First Division (Meiosis I) - The Reduction Division
- **Separates homologous chromosome pairs**
- Reduces chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n)
- Each resulting cell gets one complete set of chromosomes
- This is when crossing over occurs, creating new genetic combinations

### Second Division (Meiosis II) - The Equational Division
- **Separates sister chromatids**
- Similar to mitosis, but starting with haploid cells
- Results in four haploid cells, each with single-chromatid chromosomes
- Ensures each gamete has exactly one copy of each chromosome

## Why One Division Isn't Enough

If meiosis stopped after the first division:
- Cells would be haploid (good!)
- BUT chromosomes would still be duplicated (each consisting of two sister chromatids)
- Gametes would have twice the normal amount of DNA
- This would interfere with proper development after fertilization

## The Mathematical Necessity

- Start: One diploid cell (2n) with duplicated chromosomes
- After Meiosis I: Two haploid cells (n) with duplicated chromosomes
- After Meiosis II: Four haploid cells (n) with single-chromatid chromosomes

This two-step process ensures that when gametes fuse during fertilization, the offspring receives exactly the right amount of genetic material - one complete set from each parent.
